title: Clinically assisted nutrition and hydration in prolonged disorder of consciousness
short_description: A patient with a prolonged disorder of consciousness has no reliable prior instruction about clinically assisted nutrition and hydration, residual diagnostic uncertainty remains, and family members disagree about continuation.
decision_question: When a patient with a prolonged disorder of consciousness has no reliable prior instruction about clinically assisted nutrition and hydration, what policy should govern continuation or withdrawal?

representation.notes: Concise and detailed are controlled companion representations of one natural 2x1x2 candidate field; decision question, stipulations, candidate pools, and provenance are fixed.

jurisdiction_context: Jurisdiction-neutral ethical policy; CANH is treated as a medical intervention that may in principle be continued or withdrawn through an appropriate surrogate or best-interests process.

stipulations.statement: Repeated standardized expert disorder-of-consciousness evaluations have been completed.
stipulations.rationale: The case must not rely on a single bedside impression or avoidable diagnostic error.

stipulations.statement: Meaningful recovery is unlikely but not impossible.
stipulations.rationale: Residual uncertainty is ethically important but must not itself dictate the treatment decision.

stipulations.statement: No reliable treatment-specific prior instruction about CANH exists.
stipulations.rationale: A clear applicable advance directive would substantially change the authority structure.

stipulations.statement: CANH can sustain life long term, does not restore consciousness, and has manageable but real burdens.
stipulations.rationale: The intervention must be life-sustaining and non-restorative without being portrayed as either burden-free or intrinsically harmful.

stipulations.statement: If CANH is withdrawn, appropriate mouth care, symptom treatment, and palliative support will be provided.
stipulations.rationale: Withdrawal is evaluated as a treatment decision with ongoing care, not abandonment.

position_families: values-based withdrawal through surrogate or best-interests review
independent review when family disagreement persists
scenario: An adult suffered severe nontraumatic brain injury 14 months ago and remains dependent on clinically assisted nutrition and hydration through a gastrostomy tube. The patient is medically stable and no longer requires ventilatory or vasopressor support. For this benchmark, assume multiple serial standardized assessments by clinicians experienced in disorders of consciousness support chronic unresponsive wakefulness syndrome; meaningful recovery is unlikely but not impossible after appropriate investigation of confounders; no reliable treatment-specific prior instruction about CANH exists; CANH can sustain life for years but does not restore consciousness and carries manageable tube-related care, infection, and procedure burdens; and withdrawal would predictably lead to death with mouth care, symptom treatment, and palliative support. One close family member believes the patient strongly valued independence and would reject years of noninteractive life; another believes nutrition and hydration should continue unless there is certainty the patient cannot recover. The team must decide what policy should govern continued CANH or withdrawal.

scenario_provenance.summary: Bench-authored prolonged-disorder-of-consciousness case synthesized from AAN/ACRM/NIDILRR diagnostic guidance, nutrition-support ethics guidance, and family interview studies. It fixes serial standardized assessment, residual diagnostic/prognostic uncertainty, absence of a reliable CANH directive, non-restorative but sustaining treatment, and palliative care after withdrawal so preservation and values-based withdrawal orientations remain action-distinct.

public.text: Continue clinically assisted nutrition and hydration when prior wishes are uncertain and meaningful diagnostic or prognostic uncertainty remains, while maintaining serial specialist reassessment.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from family accounts favoring continued life-prolonging treatment, emphasizing uncertainty, and expressing symbolic or moral concern about withdrawing food and fluids. The serial-reassessment rule is a Bench operationalization rather than a literal interview policy.

public.text: Permit withdrawal of clinically assisted nutrition and hydration when a careful surrogate or best-interests process finds that continued non-restorative treatment is inconsistent with the patient's likely values and interests, with full palliative care.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from family accounts in which relatives believed the patient would not have wanted prolonged noninteractive treatment and from diverse family views about proper treatment. The formal surrogate/best-interests process is Bench policy completion.

expert.text: Use serial standardized disorder-of-consciousness assessment and an interdisciplinary benefit, burden, and patient-preference process before continuing or withdrawing clinically assisted nutrition and hydration.

provenance.summary: Adapted from convergent professional guidance emphasizing diagnostic rigor and serial assessment in prolonged disorders of consciousness and treating artificially administered nutrition and hydration as a clinical intervention subject to collaborative autonomy, benefit/burden, and ethical review. Current sources support one individualized process architecture rather than opposed professional endpoints.

framework.text: Continue nutrition and hydration when prior wishes are unknown because irreversible withdrawal should not rest on uncertain prognosis or assumptions about the value of life with profound disability.

provenance.summary: Derived from preservation of life, epistemic humility, and disability-justice reasoning. The executable continuation rule is Bench-authored.

sources.citation: AAN/ACRM/NIDILRR. Disorders of Consciousness guideline. PMID 30098791.

framework.text: Permit withdrawal when rigorous review finds continued CANH inconsistent with the person's values and unable to provide a benefit they would regard as worthwhile, while ensuring comfort care.

provenance.summary: Derived from autonomy, substituted values, proportionality, and nonabandonment. The executable withdrawal rule is Bench-authored.
